newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US senator says Swiss too biased to probe Nazi gold.
newsitem.headline: US senator says Swiss too biased to probe Nazi gold.

text.p: Swiss authorities probing charges that their banks hoarded wealth from Jews murdered by the Nazis came under new pressure on Friday when the head of a powerful U.S. banking body accused them of being biased.

Republican senator Alfonse D'Amato, whose Senate banking committee is investigating worldwide allegations that Swiss banks profited from the Holocaust, said he would put more pressure for action on three bodies created in Switzerland to investigate the fate of the Jewish funds.

In an interview with the Swiss newspaper Journal de Geneve published on Friday, he demanded a new independent commission be set up to investigate the controversy, which has led to pressure on Switzerland by campaigners in the United States, Israel and Britain.
"How can one have confidence in the Swiss authorities when they have only taken action under pressure from public opinion?," D'Amato said.
"The only means to re-establish confidence is to entrust this investigation to personalities above suspicion -- independent and non-Swiss."

Switzerland bowed to international pressure last month and set up a commission of experts to track down the missing bank accounts of murdered Jews and others who deposited money in the 1930s and 1940s to escape the attention of the Nazis.
But D'Amato said a five-year period given to the commission to carry out the task of examining bank accounts and interviewing lawyers and officials was too long.

D'Amato also voiced scepticism about the powers of an international commission set up jointly by the Swiss Bankers' Association and the World Jewish Congress to make sure Swiss banks thoroughly search their records for lost Holocaust accounts.
D'Amato said he was not sure the commission, headed by former Federal Reserve Board chairman Paul Volcker, had the power to obtain full access to all necessary bank documents and archives.
"I haven't received any clear answers to these questions," he said.
D'Amato also said he had little faith in the Swiss banking ombudsman in charge of helping nearly 1,000 claimants track down lost Holocaust accounts.
"He (the ombudsman) is Swiss. How do you expect that he'd be independent?" D'Amato said.
On Wednesday, D'Amato alleged that Swiss banks diverted money plundered from murdered Jews to compensate Swiss citizens for property nationalised by communist regimes.
At an emotional hearing in New York, he said researchers had found documents showing the Swiss struck just such a secret deal in 1949 with Poland, Hungary and Czechoslavakia.
Switzerland's foreign ministry denied the charges. But officials were combing the federal archives on Friday to make sure, a spokesman said.
"We had agreements with all countries after the war. None of those is secret," Swiss foreign ministry spokesman Jean-Philippe Tissieres told Reuters.
